rw1.passage: The bakery's owner insists that the secret to its bread is not a rare ingredient but : she lets every loaf rise for a full day, however busy the shop becomes.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw1.why: Each side gave up something, which defines a compromise. A rivalry or stalemate would mean no agreement, and a monopoly is unrelated.
rw1.passage: After months of negotiation, the two companies reached a : each gave up part of what it had wanted, and neither was entirely satisfied.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw1.why: Her earlier style contrasts with the short, plain lines of the new book, so the earlier sentences were elaborate and ornate. Terse and plain describe the new style, and hesitant does not fit elaborate.
rw1.passage: The author's earlier novels were known for elaborate, sentences, so readers were surprised that her latest book is written in short, plain lines.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw1.why: Birds that show little fear of approaching humans are unwary. Aggressive, migratory and ravenous do not explain the lack of fear.
rw1.passage: Because the island has no natural predators, its native birds have grown and show little fear of humans who approach them.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw1.why: The underlined sentence says what each partner provides, which explains how the partnership works. It does not dispute an earlier claim, compare organisms, or describe researchers.
rw1.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original science article.

Lichens, the crusty growths that cover rocks and tree bark, are not single organisms. Each is a partnership between a fungus and an alga or bacterium. The fungus provides structure and shelter, while its partner uses sunlight to make sugars that feed them both. Together, they can survive on bare rock where neither could live alone.
rw1.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It disputes the claim that lichens are single organisms.
It explains how the two partners in a lichen contribute to the arrangement.
It compares lichens with other organisms that grow on rocks.
It describes how researchers first identified the partners in a lichen.

rw1.why: Counting tiles and crushing the sheet music suggest Ravi's tension and disappointment. The text gives no reasons from the director, shows no relief, and does not discuss why he became a musician.
rw1.passage:
The following text is from an original short story. Ravi is waiting to hear the results of an audition.

Ravi had rehearsed his smile for the corridor, but when the door opened, the casting director only glanced at her clipboard and said the panel would be in touch. He walked to the lift counting the tiles under his feet: forty-one, forty-two. Outside, the afternoon traffic made an indifferent noise. He realised he was still holding the sheet music, rolled so tightly in his hand that it had begun to tear.
rw1.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe the casting director's reasons for rejecting Ravi
To show that Ravi is relieved that the audition is over
To explain why Ravi chose to become a musician
To convey Ravi's disappointment and tension through his actions after the audition

rw1.why: Text 2 suggests extra support at home may explain the scores, so the studies do not prove homework is the cause. The teacher does not say homework hurts or recommend more of it.
rw1.passage:
Text 1

Some educators argue that homework deepens learning because it requires students to practise independently what they have been taught. They point to studies in which students who completed regular assignments scored higher on end-of-year tests.

Text 2

A teacher who reviewed those studies notes that the students who did more homework were often also the ones with more support at home. She argues that, without accounting for this difference, the studies cannot show that homework itself raised scores.
rw1.q: Based on the texts, how would the teacher in Text 2 most likely respond to the educators' argument in Text 1?
choices: By saying that the studies do not rule out another explanation for the higher scores
By arguing that students who do homework perform worse on tests
By agreeing that homework is the only cause of the higher scores
By claiming that students should be given more homework

rw1.why: The text describes replay of daily activity during sleep and better recall after sleeping, so sleep helps consolidate learning. It contradicts the idea of an inactive brain, and nothing suggests sleep matters less than studying.
rw1.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay about sleep.

We often treat sleep as downtime, a pause between periods of real activity. But researchers who monitor the sleeping brain find that it is anything but idle: during certain stages, patterns of neural activity from the day are replayed, as though the brain were rehearsing what it has learned. Students who slept after studying a list of words recalled more of them the next day than students who stayed awake for the same period.
rw1.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Sleep is less important to learning than studying.
The brain is entirely inactive while a person sleeps.
Sleep is an active process that helps the brain consolidate what has been learned.
Students should study the same list of words every day.

rw1.why: The text contrasts the village's look of stillness with a record of fires, a shifting river and emigration, and calls the stillness the result of recoveries. It does not predict disappearance, or say anything about visitors' reading or the mill's success.
rw1.passage:
The following text is from an original essay about a village's history.

The village of Hallow End has been described by visitors as unchanging, a place where nothing has happened for centuries. The parish records tell another story: the church burned down twice, the river changed course in 1740, leaving the mill stranded, and the population fell by half during a single decade of emigration. What looks like stillness, the essayist suggests, is the surface left by repeated recoveries.
rw1.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The village of Hallow End has lost most of its population and may soon disappear.
A village that seems unchanged has in fact been shaped by repeated upheaval and recovery.
Visitors to Hallow End rarely read the parish records.
The river's changed course made the mill more successful.

rw1.why: Rapid growth in spring is shown by the rise from 120 in March to 310 in May, which the first choice reports. The others reverse the trend, list extremes without the rise, or cover a slower period.
rw1.passage: A city planner counted the number of cyclists who crossed a bridge on the first Monday of each month from January to May. She wants to emphasise how quickly numbers rose in spring.
rw1.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the text?
choices: the number of cyclists crossing the bridge fell from 310 in March to 120 in May.
the number of cyclists crossing the bridge was 310 in May, the highest of the five months, and 60 in January.
the number of cyclists crossing the bridge rose from 60 in January to 120 in March.
the number of cyclists crossing the bridge rose from 120 in March to 310 in May, more than doubling in two months.

rw1.why: The change is shown by the later date of mid-March compared with the first week of April, and only the first quotation gives the later arrival. The others describe the record keeping or the earlier date alone.
rw1.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay about a naturalist.

The naturalist Cornelia Voss kept careful records of the birds in her garden for forty years. In the 1970s she began to notice that the spring arrival of swallows, which had once come in the first week of April, was creeping earlier. By the 1990s they were arriving in the middle of March.
rw1.q: A student claims that Voss's records documented a change in the timing of swallows' arrival. Which quotation from the text best supports the student's claim?
choices: "By the 1990s they were arriving in the middle of March."
"The naturalist Cornelia Voss kept careful records of the birds in her garden for forty years."
"swallows, which had once come in the first week of April"

rw1.why: Higher attention scores in the group that practised an instrument support the claim. The age of the children and the length of the lessons do not show an effect on attention.
rw1.passage:
A researcher claims that practising a musical instrument improves a child's attention in other tasks.

A study followed two groups of eight-year-olds for a year. One group took weekly piano lessons, and the other took weekly art lessons. At the end of the year, the children who had played piano scored higher on a test of sustained attention than the art group.
rw1.q: Which finding from the text most directly supports the researcher's claim?
choices: Both groups were made up of eight-year-olds.
The piano group scored higher than the art group on a test of sustained attention.
The children had weekly lessons throughout the year.
The art group was taught by an experienced teacher.

rw1.why: If reefs host a quarter of species on a tiny area, then protecting them can sustain many species. The text does not support the claims that protection has no effect or needs a large area.
rw1.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original science article.

Coral reefs host a quarter of marine species yet cover less than one percent of the ocean floor. When a reef bleaches and dies, fish that depend on it for food and shelter disappear within a few years. This suggests that protecting a small area of reef
rw1.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: is unlikely to affect any fish.
would harm species that live in deep water.
may help sustain a large number of species.
is useful only if it covers a large area.

rw1.why: Higher levels near the airport suggest noise may contribute, while the caution means it is not the only factor. The other choices overstate the findings.
rw1.passage:
The following text is from an original essay about urban noise.

Researchers measured the stress hormones of residents on two streets with similar populations, one near an airport and one far from it. The residents of the street near the airport showed consistently higher levels. The researchers cautioned that other differences between the two streets might also play a role. Still, the results suggest that
rw1.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: aircraft noise is the only cause of stress in cities.
aircraft noise may be one factor affecting the stress of those who live nearby.
people far from airports experience no stress at all.
stress hormones are unrelated to the environment.

rw1.why: The subject is the plural roses, so the present tense verb bloom agrees. Blooms and has bloomed are singular, and blooming is not a finite verb.
rw1.passage: The garden's roses, which were planted in 1890, every June.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.why: The relative pronoun is the subject of the verb had played, so who is correct, and the clause needs the verb had. The other choices use the wrong pronoun or omit the verb.
rw1.passage: The team's captain, played in three national finals, was asked to lead the training session.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.why: The second clause contrasts with the first, so although is the right conjunction.
rw1.passage: The report concluded that the new drug was effective, several patients experienced side effects.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.passage: Ellis wanted to learn to dive, the wreck near his home.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.passage: The sanctuary cares for injured animals, and volunteers feed them twice daily.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.passage: The report, along with its appendices, available on the council's website.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

rw1.passage: The new phone's battery is smaller than its predecessor's. the device runs for longer between charges, thanks to a more efficient processor.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

rw1.why: The second sentence introduces a different use of honey, so However is a suitable transition in this context. Thus and For example do not fit.
rw1.passage: Honey is prized as a sweetener. it has also long been used as a wound dressing, because it draws moisture from the surrounding tissue and slows the growth of bacteria.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

rw1.why: The minority view contrasts with the majority, so Still is the best transition.
rw1.passage: Surveys show that most students prefer to study at home. a significant minority say they concentrate better in a library.
rw1.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

rw1.why: To introduce her work, the choice must say who she is and what she studies, which the first choice does. The others give a workplace, a date or a general fact.
rw1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Dr. Yara Nasser is a marine biologist.
  • She studies how sea turtles navigate.
  • She has tracked more than 200 turtles with satellite tags.
  • Her research was published in 2021.
  • She works at a university in Lisbon.

The student wants to introduce a person to an audience that is unfamiliar with her work.
rw1.q: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Yara Nasser works at a university in Lisbon.
Marine biologist Yara Nasser, who studies how sea turtles navigate, has tracked more than 200 of them with satellite tags.
Dr. Yara Nasser published her research in 2021.
Sea turtles have been tracked by satellite tags.

rw1.why: The goal is to explain the tool's purpose, so the choice should describe what it measures and how sailors use it, which the first choice does.
rw1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • A sextant is a navigational instrument.
  • It measures the angle between the horizon and a celestial body.
  • Sailors use that angle to calculate their latitude.
  • The sextant was invented in the 1700s.
  • It replaced the older octant.

The student wants to explain the purpose of a tool.
rw1.q: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: A sextant measures the angle between the horizon and a celestial body, which sailors use to calculate their latitude.
The sextant, invented in the 1700s, replaced the older octant.
A sextant is a navigational instrument invented in the 1700s.
Sailors have used many instruments to find their position.

rw1.why: A comparison needs the shared feature and a contrast between them, which the first choice supplies. The others describe one city or give separate facts.
rw1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Reykjavik has a population of about 140,000.
  • Valletta has a population of about 6,000.
  • Reykjavik is the capital of Iceland.
  • Valletta is the capital of Malta.
  • Both are coastal capitals.

The student wants to make a comparison between two cities.
rw1.q: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Reykjavik is the capital of Iceland, and Valletta is the capital of Malta.
Reykjavik has a population of about 140,000.
Valletta, with a population of about 6,000, is a coastal city.

rw2h.why: The court once required a warrant and now does not, so the ruling reverses its earlier stance. Reaffirmation and clarification would keep the position, and postponement does not fit the change.
rw2h.passage: The ruling was widely read as a of the court's earlier position: where the justices had once insisted that such searches required a warrant, they now held that no warrant was needed.
rw2h.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw2h.why: Short plain sentences are unadorned, and deceptively signals that the plainness hides effort. Labyrinthine, ostentatious and turgid all describe ornate or complicated writing.
rw2h.passage: The novelist's prose is deceptively : its short, plain sentences seem effortless, yet each one conceals a long process of revision and a precise choice of rhythm.
rw2h.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw2h.why: The contrast with the faded manuscript shows that the vault-stored colours stayed bright, which vivid means. Muted would describe faded colours, and nothing suggests the colours were unstable or ordinary.
rw2h.passage: Because the manuscript had been stored in a sealed vault, its colours were still remarkably after six centuries, while those of a similar manuscript left on open shelves had faded almost entirely.
rw2h.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw2h.why: She acknowledged offence without admitting regret, which is evasive. Unreserved and heartfelt describe sincere apologies, and nothing in the passage concerns timing.
rw2h.passage: The politician's apology was widely seen as : she admitted that the remarks had caused offence but declined to say whether she regretted making them.
rw2h.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

rw2h.why: The underlined sentence says the doctrine of perfect spheres made the mountainous moon unwelcome, which explains the resistance described. It does not describe the telescope's construction or argue for the doctrine.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay about the history of the telescope.

When Galileo first turned his telescope to the night sky in 1609, he saw mountains on the moon. This was not, at first, a welcome discovery. The prevailing doctrine held that heavenly bodies were perfect spheres, and a cratered, mountainous moon was an affront to it. Galileo's critics did not deny that the instrument magnified; they denied that what it showed could be trusted.
rw2h.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It describes how Galileo made his telescope.
It argues that heavenly bodies are perfect spheres.
It compares Galileo's discovery with earlier ones.
It explains why an observation was met with resistance.

rw2h.why: The sentence turns from Joaquín's childhood memory to the evidence of neglect, from which he infers his father's decline. The text does not blame the agent, give his reason for selling or say when he last visited.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is from an original novel. Joaquín has returned to the town where he grew up to sell his late father's shop.

The shop had always smelled of machine oil and tea, and for a moment, as the bell rang above the door, Joaquín was nine again, standing on a crate to reach the counter. Then he saw the dust. It lay on the shelves in a fine grey skin, undisturbed, and he understood that his father's last months had been spent in the back room while the front quietly gave up. The estate agent, waiting by the window, asked whether he would like to see the figures. Joaquín said he would, and did not move.
rw2h.q: Which choice best describes the function of the sentence beginning "Then he saw the dust" in the text as a whole?
choices: It marks the shift from Joaquín's memory of the shop to a realisation about his father's decline.
It shows that the estate agent has neglected the shop.
It explains why Joaquín decided to sell the shop.
It suggests that Joaquín has not been to the shop since childhood.

rw2h.why: Text 2 found employment moved in step across the border, which does not match the fall in jobs that Text 1 predicts. It does not support abolition, and does not discuss pay above the minimum.
rw2h.passage:
Text 1

Some economists argue that minimum wage increases reduce employment because they raise the cost of labour. If employers must pay more for each worker, they will hire fewer workers or reduce hours.

Text 2

A labour economist reports on a study of neighbouring counties on either side of a state border, one of which raised its minimum wage. She found that employment in the two counties moved in step before and after the increase, and she suggests that employers may respond to higher wages in ways that do not involve cutting jobs, such as raising prices or accepting lower turnover costs.
rw2h.q: Based on the texts, how would the economist in Text 2 most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that employers always reduce workers' hours
By arguing that the minimum wage should be abolished
By claiming that employers pay workers more than the minimum wage
By pointing out that evidence from the border counties does not match the effect Text 1 predicts

rw2h.why: The text reports that rivers in parks without wolves also recovered and urges caution in crediting wolves, so the analysis challenges the assumption. It does not say wolves have no effect on deer, that recovery needs wet years, or that wolves harmed rivers.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original science article.

For years, ecologists assumed that wolves reintroduced to a park would improve the health of its rivers only indirectly, by reducing the number of grazing deer and so allowing streamside trees to recover. A new analysis suggests the effect may be smaller than claimed. Rivers in comparable parks without wolves also recovered over the same period, apparently because a series of wet years restored the water table, and the study's authors urge caution in crediting any single cause.
rw2h.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Wolves have no effect on the numbers of deer in a park.
A new analysis challenges the assumption that wolves were chiefly responsible for the recovery of the parks' rivers.
Rivers recover only when the water table is restored by wet years.
Ecologists agree that reintroducing wolves has harmed rivers.

rw2h.why: The text says Marchetti rejects the minimalist label because her spareness serves the light, which she treats as her main material. She uses light, the galleries change, and she is described as a minimalist.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay about an architect.

The architect Delphine Marchetti is often described as a minimalist, but she rejects the label. Her buildings are spare, she says, not because she values emptiness but because she wants nothing to distract from the light, which she treats as her principal material. In her best-known museum, the walls carry no ornament, yet the ceilings are pierced with openings of varying sizes so that the galleries change from hour to hour.
rw2h.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Marchetti's spare designs serve her interest in light rather than a belief in emptiness.
Marchetti rejects the use of light in her buildings.
Marchetti's museum was designed to remain the same throughout the day.
Marchetti is widely thought to be a maximalist.

In July, algae covered 48 percent of the lake near the farm, up from 20 percent in May.
In July, algae covered 48 percent of the lake near the farm but only 12 percent of the forest lake.
Algae covered more of each lake in July than in January.

rw2h.why: Magnifying swings means a self-reinforcing process in both directions, which the last sentence states directly. The other quotations state her thesis or one step in the cycle without showing the full swing.
rw2h.passage:
The following text is adapted from an original essay about an economist.

The economist Odile Fontaine argued that markets are less self-correcting than is commonly assumed. A boom, she wrote, tends to persuade investors that prices will keep rising, and their buying is what drives the prices higher; the process feeds itself until it exhausts the supply of buyers, at which point the same logic runs in reverse.
rw2h.q: A student claims that, in Fontaine's view, markets can magnify their own swings. Which quotation from the text best supports the student's claim?
choices: "The economist Odile Fontaine argued that markets are less self-correcting than is commonly assumed."
"A boom, she wrote, tends to persuade investors that prices will keep rising"
"their buying is what drives the prices higher"
"the process feeds itself until it exhausts the supply of buyers, at which point the same logic runs in reverse"

rw2h.why: If fish thrive once placed in a high lake, then conditions there are suitable and only the barrier of waterfalls explains their absence. The other findings do not isolate waterfalls as the cause.

A student is researching why some mountain lakes have no fish.

The ecologist Hana Reyes reports that lakes above 3,000 metres in the study area contained no fish, even though they had suitable temperatures and plenty of insects. Each of those lakes is separated from lower waters by waterfalls steeper than any fish can climb.

choices: Fish introduced by hikers to one high lake soon became established and thrived.
The high lakes freeze for several months each winter.
Insects in the high lakes are smaller than those in lower lakes.
Several of the high lakes were formed by glaciers.

choices: a name for the neighbouring site.
a unit of measure for grain.
a word that cannot be translated.
a numeral used only in lists.

rw2h.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?

whether the frame is made of steel.
how well the material tolerates repeated flexing.
how quickly the frame can be made.
